title: A flame speed is set by reaction rate and diffusion: S_L scales as the square root of their product
summary: A premixed flame is a wave that heats the fresh gas by conduction until it reacts. Balancing the heating against the heat release gives the scaling S_L ~ sqrt(alpha times reaction rate), which explains the bell curve in equivalence ratio and the strain rate at which a flame dies.

media.alt: Line plot of laminar flame speed in cm/s against equivalence ratio from 0.55 to 1.6, three bell-shaped model curves for 0, 10 and 20 percent nitrogen dilution peaking near phi 1.07 at about 39, 32 and 25 cm/s, with open markers and error bars for experiment lying close to the curves.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F9.2 with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery), not a project result.

source.note: Standard combustion theory (thermal flame theory in the Mallard and Le Chatelier tradition; strain and Damkohler arguments). The flame speeds, adiabatic flame temperatures and the scaling test were computed here with Cantera 3.1 and GRI-Mech 3.0 for methane-air at 300 K and 1 atm; they are illustrations of the theory, not experimental values. The figure is the design system's synthetic F9.2 render.

read_the_figure.question: Does the model reproduce the measured laminar flame speed across equivalence ratio, and how does dilution change it?
read_the_figure.axes: x: equivalence ratio phi (1 is stoichiometric, left lean, right rich). y: laminar flame speed S_L in cm/s on a linear axis, so a vertical distance is a difference in speed.
look_at: The bell: S_L peaks slightly on the rich side of 1 and falls on both sides, faster on the lean side.
Open markers with error bars are experiment, lines are the model; check whether the bars reach the line, not only whether the markers are near it.
The ordering of the three curves: more dilution lowers the whole bell without moving its peak much.
The flanks: the largest model-to-experiment gaps usually sit where S_L is small and most sensitive, at the very lean and very rich ends.
read_the_figure.proves: Model curves passing through the error bars across the whole phi range and for each dilution is evidence that the chemistry and transport together give the right burning rate.
if_wrong: A model line systematically above the markers at one end: reaction rates or transport are off there.
Markers scattering by more than their bars: the stated uncertainty omits a source, such as the stretch correction.
Experiment values that include stretch effects compared with a model that is stretch-free: the comparison is not like for like.
must_check: Unburned temperature and pressure for every series.
Whether the experimental S_L is the unstretched (zero-stretch) value.
Fuel and oxidiser purity and the dilution definition.
Error bars given and their meaning: one standard deviation or an expanded interval.

terms.meaning: A flame in a gas where fuel and oxidiser are already mixed before burning. It propagates as a wave into the fresh mixture.
The speed at which an unstretched planar flame moves relative to the unburned gas. It is a property of the mixture, temperature and pressure.
The region ahead of the reaction, where conduction warms the fresh gas and no appreciable heat is released.
The thin region where most of the heat is released.
The conductivity divided by density and specific heat: how fast temperature differences spread.
The reciprocal of the chemical time: the fraction of the temperature rise completed per second in the reaction zone.
Fuel-to-air ratio relative to the stoichiometric one: 1 stoichiometric, below 1 lean, above 1 rich.
The velocity gradient along the flame surface-normal that stretches the flow: a = -du/dx at the stagnation plane of a counterflow.
The fractional rate of change of flame surface area: it combines strain and curvature.
The ratio of the flow time to the chemical time. Large: chemistry keeps up. Order one: the flame is near extinction.
The strain rate above which a counterflow flame can no longer exist.

remember: Flame thickness: delta = alpha / S_L. Flame time: delta / S_L = alpha / S_L^2.
Scaling: S_L ~ sqrt(alpha times omega-bar). Double the reaction rate, S_L goes up by 1.41.
Arrhenius inside: S_L ~ exp(-E_a / (2 R T_b)), the half comes from the square root.
S_L against phi is a bell, with its peak slightly rich of 1 for methane, and falling faster on the lean side.
Extinction scaling: a_ext ~ S_L^2 / alpha, so it is twice as sensitive to chemistry as S_L is.

understand.title: A flame is a balance, not a thing
understand.text: Ahead of the reaction the fresh gas must be warmed by conduction against the incoming flow. If the reaction is fast, the zone is thin and the front can advance faster. If diffusion is fast, the heat reaches farther ahead and again the front advances faster. The geometric mean of the two sets the speed.

understand.title: A scaling is not a formula
understand.text: The argument gives the dependence on alpha and omega-bar and the exponent one half, but not the numerical prefactor. The prefactor needs the asymptotic analysis of the reaction layer. Use the scaling to understand trends and to check a model's behaviour, not to predict an absolute S_L.

understand.title: Why flames die in a strained flow
understand.text: Strain shortens the time a fluid element spends in the flame. When that time becomes comparable to the chemical time, the flame cannot burn the fresh gas it is fed and goes out abruptly, not gradually.

steps.title: The steady one-dimensional flame
steps.note: In a frame fixed to the front the fresh gas arrives at S_L. Convection of enthalpy on the left, conduction and heat release q-dot on the right. This one equation holds the whole scaling argument.

steps.title: The preheat zone is an exponential
steps.note: Ahead of the reaction (x < 0), convection balances conduction and the solution decays upstream with the length alpha / S_L (verified symbolically; T_i is the temperature where reaction begins). A faster flame has a thinner preheat zone.

steps.title: Energy balance across the flame
steps.note: Integrate the equation over the flame: the conduction terms vanish at both ends, leaving enthalpy carried in equals heat released. With q-dot written as rho c_p (T_b - T_u) times the mean rate omega-bar and a reaction-zone thickness of order delta, the heat released per area is of that size.

steps.title: Combine the two: S_L scales as the square root
steps.note: A scaling: equal up to a factor of order one. A real test of it: multiplying every rate in GRI-Mech by 4 at fixed thermodynamics and transport raises the computed S_L of a stoichiometric methane flame by exactly 2.0000. The speed is proportional to the square root of the rate.

steps.title: Put the Arrhenius law inside omega-bar
steps.note: Burning happens near the hot end, so the rate is evaluated at the flame temperature (verified symbolically). The square root halves the activation energy seen by S_L. With an assumed E_a = 150 kJ/mol, raising T_b from 2000 to 2050 K raises S_L by 11.6 percent, compared with 24.6 percent if the rate itself were the measured quantity.

steps.title: The bell in equivalence ratio
steps.note: The flame temperature rises toward stoichiometric and falls on both sides. Computed here for methane-air at 300 K and 1 atm: S_L = 0.116, 0.275, 0.381, 0.385, 0.337, 0.141 m/s at phi = 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.4, with T_ad = 1666, 2001, 2231, 2212, 2131, 1979 K. Treating the lean side as the scaling gives an effective E_a of about 105 to 143 kJ/mol, the right order for such chemistry. In these values S_L peaks near phi = 1.1 while T_ad peaks near 1.0: the simple scaling does not capture that, because omega-bar and alpha also change with composition.

steps.title: Flame thickness and the time it takes
steps.note: The flame time is the chemical time. This is what a strained flow has to be compared with in the next steps.

steps.title: Strain in a counterflow and the extinction scaling
steps.note: Two opposed nozzles make a stagnation plane where the axial velocity falls linearly; a is the slope, in 1/s. For nozzles a distance L apart with outflow speed V, a linear profile gives a of order 2V/L; the exact prefactor depends on the nozzle boundary conditions. A flame that spends 1/a in the flame zone survives while that time exceeds the chemical time, so extinction occurs at Da of order one. Since S_L squared goes as exp(-E_a / R T_b), a_ext is twice as sensitive to chemistry as S_L.

steps.title: Comparing with experiment
steps.note: Experiments measure a flame speed at finite stretch and extrapolate to zero stretch, which adds an uncertainty. A model agrees with experiment when most normalised residuals z fall within plus or minus 2 and show no trend with phi. The plot should have error bars on the measured points and the same unburned state for model and data (F9.2, F9.3).

worked.title: How thin is the flame, and how fast is its chemistry?
worked.problem: For stoichiometric methane-air at 300 K and 1 atm the computed flame speed is S_L = 0.381 m/s and the cold-gas thermal diffusivity is alpha = 2.25e-5 m^2/s. Estimate the flame thickness and the mean reaction rate from the scaling, and compare with the thermal thickness found in the full calculation, 0.439 mm.

solution.text: Mean reaction rate from S_L squared over alpha.

worked.answer: The scaling gives delta = 0.06 mm and a flame time of 0.16 ms, but the computed thermal thickness is 0.44 mm, 7.4 times larger. The scaling used the cold-gas alpha; in the flame the hot gas has a much larger diffusivity, so the effective alpha is bigger. The scaling gives the right way things depend on each other, not the absolute size.

analyze.q: Double the pressure of a flame. The density doubles while the conductivity and c_p hardly change, so alpha halves. If the mean reaction rate omega-bar per second were unchanged, what would the scaling give for S_L and the flame thickness, and what else would you need to know to say more?
analyze.hint: alpha is proportional to 1/rho; how omega-bar changes depends on the reaction order.

analyze.q: A lean flame at phi = 0.6 has S_L of 0.12 m/s. Using S_L^2 / alpha as an estimate of a_ext, how would you expect its extinction strain rate to compare with that of a stoichiometric flame, and why?

The Arrhenius slope of ln S_L against 1/T_b is -E_a/2R. A group fits a slope giving E_a of 100 kJ/mol and another uses the same data but assumes S_L is proportional to the rate. What E_a does the second group obtain?
analyze.hint: Their slope is E_a/R, not E_a/2R.

evaluate.q: A mechanism over-predicts S_L at phi = 0.7 by 15 percent but matches at phi = 1.0. The scaling says S_L depends on the square root of the rate. By how much would you adjust the rate of the controlling chain-branching step to fix it, and what else would you check first?
evaluate.hint: Required rate change is 1.15 squared. Check transport data and the stretch correction first.

evaluate.q: Is agreement of the model with measured flame speed enough to trust it for extinction, ignition and emissions?
evaluate.hint: S_L tests one combination of rates and diffusion. Each other target tests different pathways.

create: Plan a validation plot for a new fuel: which three series would you measure (S_L against phi at one pressure, a_ext at one phi, and what third?), and what would the figure need so a reader can judge agreement?
Write a small program that takes S_L(phi) and T_ad(phi) arrays and fits E_eff through ln S_L against 1/T_ad, with a bootstrap interval on the slope.

checks.q: Why is the preheat zone thickness alpha / S_L and not some other combination?
checks.hint: Balance S_L times T prime against alpha times T double prime.
checks.answer: Ahead of the reaction there is no source, so convection of enthalpy balances conduction: S_L T' = alpha T''. The solution is an exponential with decay length alpha / S_L. Only that combination of alpha (m^2/s) and S_L (m/s) has the dimension of length.

checks.q: A flame has S_L = 0.40 m/s and alpha = 2.0e-5 m^2/s. Find the thickness, the mean reaction rate and the flame time.
checks.hint: delta = alpha / S_L; omega-bar = S_L^2 / alpha.
checks.answer: delta = 2.0e-5 / 0.40 = 5.0e-5 m = 0.05 mm. omega-bar = 0.16 / 2.0e-5 = 8.0e3 per second. Flame time 1/omega-bar = 0.125 ms. These are scaling estimates, good to a factor of a few.

checks.q: A mixture's flame temperature drops from 2200 K to 2000 K. With E_a = 150 kJ/mol, by what factor does S_L fall according to the scaling, and by what factor does a_ext fall?
checks.hint: S_L is proportional to exp(-E_a / 2 R T); a_ext to S_L squared.
checks.answer: ln(S_L ratio) = (E_a / 2R)(1/2200 - 1/2000) = 9017 x (-4.545e-5) = -0.410, so S_L falls by a factor 0.66 (to 66 percent). a_ext goes as its square: 0.44, falling to 44 percent. Extinction is the more sensitive observable.

checks.q: A paper reports a flame speed measured in a spherical expanding flame at a single radius and compares it directly with a model's S_L. What is wrong?
checks.answer: The expanding flame is stretched (curvature and strain), so the measured speed is not the unstretched S_L the model computes. The measurement should be extrapolated to zero stretch, with the extrapolation uncertainty included. Without that, differences of a few cm/s are not interpretable.

checks.q: You have a model and a counterflow rig. How do you design the extinction experiment so the comparison is fair?
checks.hint: Define the strain rate, state boundary conditions, repeat.
checks.answer: Report the same strain-rate definition for both (model and experiment, for instance the velocity gradient upstream of the flame), state nozzle boundary conditions and separation, increase the flow in small steps, record the last burning condition and the first extinguished one so that a_ext is a bracket, and repeat several times to give an interval. In the model, run the same boundary conditions and step the strain until the solution drops to the non-burning branch.

provenance.notes: Standard theory. The preheat solution and the scaling algebra were checked with sympy; the rate-multiplier test, flame speeds and thickness were computed with Cantera 3.1 (GRI-Mech 3.0). The image opened was the synthetic F9.2 reference render. The extinction argument is a scaling only. No project measurement or unpublished number is used.
